## 4.1 Empirical variogram of the raw response

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

geo_data <- geoR::as.geodata(
  litho2,
  coords.col = match(c("Easting", "Northing"), names(litho2)),
  data.col = match("log_Thickness", names(litho2)),
  covar.col = match(
    c("Surf_Elevation", "AB_Elevation"),
    names(litho2)
  )
)

maximum_distance <- max(
  dist(litho2[, c("Easting", "Northing")])
) * 0.60

variog_raw <- geoR::variog(
  geo_data,
  max.dist = maximum_distance
)

plot(
  variog_raw,
  main = "Empirical variogram of log thickness"
)
```

## 4.2 NON-SPATIAL LINEAR MODEL

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

lm_model <- lm(
  log_Thickness ~ Surf_Elevation_scaled + AB_Elevation_scaled,
  data = litho2
)

print(summary(lm_model))
```

## 4.3 A residual variogram is more appropriate when covariate trends are present.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

residual_data <- data.frame(
  Easting = litho2$Easting,
  Northing = litho2$Northing,
  residual = residuals(lm_model)
)

geo_residuals <- geoR::as.geodata(
  residual_data,
  coords.col = 1:2,
  data.col = 3
)

variog_residuals <- geoR::variog(
  geo_residuals,
  max.dist = maximum_distance
)

plot(
  variog_residuals,
  main = "Variogram of non-spatial model residuals"
)

```

# 5 The linear spatial model

The model assumes:

$$Y = X\beta + W + \varepsilon$$

Where:

- $Y$: Response variable ($n \times 1$)
- $X$: Design matrix ($n \times p$) of covariates
- $\beta$: Regression coefficients ($p \times 1$)
- $W$: Spatial random effects ($n \times 1$) with $W \sim \mathcal{MVN}(0, \sigma^2 R(\phi))$
- $\varepsilon$: Independent errors with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{MVN}(0, \tau^2 I)$


This is the hierarchy of spatial model



- Level 1: DATA MODEL (Likelihood)

$$
Y(s) = X(s)\boldsymbol{\beta} + W(s) + \varepsilon(s)
$$

$$
\varepsilon(s) \sim N(0, \tau^2)
$$

This is what we observe.

- Level 2: PROCESS MODEL (Prior for $W$)

$$
W(s) \sim \operatorname{GP}\left(0, \sigma^2 R(\phi)\right)
$$

This is the underlying spatial process.

- Level 3: PARAMETER MODEL (Hyperpriors)

$$
\sigma^2 \sim \operatorname{IG}(a_\sigma, b_\sigma)
$$

$$
\phi \sim \operatorname{Gamma}(a_\phi, b_\phi)
$$

This is what we don't know.


## 5.1 Spatial Correlation Functions

The spatial correlation matrix $R(\phi)$ depends on the distance between locations:

### Exponential Correlation:

$$R(\phi)_{ij} = \exp\left(-\frac{d_{ij}}{\phi}\right)$$

### Matérn Correlation (with $\kappa = 1.5$):

$$R(\phi)_{ij} = \left(1 + \frac{d_{ij}}{\phi}\right) \exp\left(-\frac{d_{ij}}{\phi}\right)$$

Where $d_{ij}$ is the distance between locations $i$ and $j$, and $\phi$ is the spatial range parameter.

# 6 Prior Distributions

The function uses conjugate priors:

## Regression Coefficients ($\beta$)

$$\beta \sim \mathcal{MVN}(\beta_{\text{mean}}, \beta_{\text{var}} \cdot I)$$ Where $\beta_{\text{mean}} = 0$ and $\beta_{\text{var}} = 1000$ (vague prior)

## Spatial Variance ($\sigma^2$)

$$\sigma^2 \sim \text{Inverse-Gamma}(\alpha_{\sigma} = 2, \beta_{\sigma} = 1)$$

## Error Variance ($\tau^2$)

$$\tau^2 \sim \text{Inverse-Gamma}(\alpha_{\tau} = 2, \beta_{\tau} = 1)$$

## Spatial Range ($\phi$)

$$\phi \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha_{\phi} = 2, \beta_{\phi} = 1)$$

# 7 Helper functions

## 7.1 The rmvn_precision\` Function

```{r, eval=FALSE}
rmvn_precision <- function(precision, linear_term) {
# precision: = Q (posterior precision)

#   linear_term:b = coefficient of β in the linear term of log-posterior
#   = XᵀY/σ² + P₀μ₀
#   = evidence from data + evidence from prior
# 
# This b is NOT the regression coefficient β itself,
# but rather the COEFFICIENT that multiplies β in the log-posterior
#   
  
  U <- chol(precision)
  # This gives μ = Q⁻¹b (mean of the coefficients β), for cholesky we use forward and backward two steps to solve this equation for μ
  posterior_mean <- backsolve(U, forwardsolve(t(U), linear_term))
  
 
  # This generates random β ~ N(μ, Q⁻¹)
  random_part <- backsolve(U, rnorm(length(linear_term)))
  
   # Each sample is a draw of β (the regression coefficients!)
  as.numeric(posterior_mean + random_part)
```

This function samples from a multivariate normal distribution parameterized by its **precision matrix** (inverse covariance matrix):

$$X \sim \mathcal{N}(Q^{-1}b, Q^{-1})$$ Note: this function can also be used for any other parameter whose posterior has the precision-form normal distribution

$$\theta \mid -\sim N(Q^{-1}\mathbf{b}, Q^{-1})$$ including spatial random effect $w$ when its full conditional is expressed in this form.

## 7.2 Bayesian Linear Regression Model

For the Bayesian linear regression model, assume the following prior distribution:

$$\boldsymbol{\beta}
\sim
N\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_0,\mathbf{P}_0^{-1}\right),$$

where $\mathbf{P}_0$ is the prior precision matrix.

The likelihood is:

$$\mathbf{Y}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta}
\sim
N\left(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}\right).$$

The posterior distribution is:

$$\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\mathbf{Y}
\sim
N\left(\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{b},\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\right),$$

where

$$\mathbf{Q}
=
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}}{\sigma^2}
+\mathbf{P}_0$$

is the **posterior precision matrix**, and

$$\mathbf{b}
=
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{Y}}{\sigma^2}
+\mathbf{P}_0\boldsymbol{\mu}_0$$

is the **posterior linear term**.

Therefore, the posterior mean and covariance matrix are:

$$E\left(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\mathbf{Y}\right)
=\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{b},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}\left(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\mathbf{Y}\right)
=\mathbf{Q}^{-1}.$$

## 7.3 Understanding Cholesky factorization

```{r, eval=FALSE}
posterior_mean <- backsolve(U, forwardsolve(t(U), linear_term))
```

This single line of code solves the linear system

$$\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbf{b}$$

for $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ using Cholesky factorization, where:

$$\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{U}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{U}$$

is the precision matrix,

$$\mathbf{b} = \mathtt{linear\_term}$$

is the posterior linear term, and

$$\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathtt{posterior\_mean}$$

is the quantity we want to calculate.

### 7.3.1 Mathematical Goal

We want to solve:

$$\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbf{b}.$$

Substituting $\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{U}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{U}$ gives:

$$\mathbf{U}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbf{b}.$$

### 7.3.2 Two-Step Solution Strategy

Instead of explicitly calculating $\mathbf{Q}^{-1}$, we use two triangular solves.

#### Step 1: Solve for $\mathbf{z}$

Solve

$$\mathbf{U}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{b}$$

for $\mathbf{z}$:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
z <- forwardsolve(t(U), linear_term)
```

Because $\mathbf{U}$ is upper triangular, $\mathbf{U}^{\mathsf T}$ is lower triangular, so `forwardsolve()` is used.

#### Step 2: Solve for $\boldsymbol{\mu}$

Solve

$$\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbf{z}$$

for $\boldsymbol{\mu}$:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
posterior_mean <- backsolve(U, z)
```

Because $\mathbf{U}$ is upper triangular, `backsolve()` is used.

#### Combined into One Line

The two steps can be combined as:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
posterior_mean <- backsolve(
  U,
  forwardsolve(t(U), linear_term)
)
```

Therefore,

$$\boldsymbol{\mu}
=\mathbf{U}^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{-\mathsf T}\mathbf{b}
=\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$$

This approach is more numerically stable and efficient than explicitly calculating $\mathbf{Q}^{-1}$.

Of course we can solve the equation without Cholesky, but it will be expensive.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
posterior_mean <- solve(Q, b)  # O(n³) - expensive!
```

## 7.4 Another helper function.

This function is quite simple. It is used to calculate the spatial correlation matrix using either the exponential or Matérn correlation ($\kappa=1.5$) function.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
 #  Spatial correlation matrix
  make_correlation <- function(phi) {
    if (!is.finite(phi) || phi <= 0) {
      stop("phi must be positive and finite.")
    }

    if (cov_family == "exponential") {
      R <- exp(-distance_matrix / phi)
    } else if (cov_family == "matern") {
      R <- geoR::matern(
        distance_matrix,
        phi = phi,
        kappa = 1.5
      )
    } else {
      stop("Use cov_family = 'exponential' or 'matern'.")
    }

    # A tiny diagonal jitter protects Cholesky decompositions from rounding
    # problems 
    # It is not the nugget variance tau2-it's purely a computational trick
    R + diag(1e-8, n)
  }

```

# 8 Main MCMC function to run data analysis

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# MCMC FUNCTION ----------------------------------------------------------

run_spatial_mcmc <- function(
    data,
    response,
    covariates,
    coords,
    n_iter = 10000,
    burnin = 5000,
    thin = 5,
    cov_family = "exponential",
    priors = list(
      beta_mean = 0,
      beta_var = 1000,
      sigma2_shape = 2,
      sigma2_rate = 1,
      tau2_shape = 2,
      tau2_rate = 1,
      phi_shape = 2,
      phi_rate = 1
    ),
    initial_values = list(
      beta = NULL,
      W = NULL,
      sigma2 = 0.5,
      tau2 = 0.2,
      phi = 1
    ),
    phi_proposal_sd = 0.15,  #This is the standard deviation of the proposal distribution used in the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm 
                             #for the spatial range parameter ϕ,It controls how large the steps are when proposing new values of ϕ.
    progress_every = 100     #This controls how often the MCMC algorithm prints progress updates to the console during the simulation.
) {                          #i.e we will see Iteration: 100 Iteration: 200 Iteration: 300, ...

  # Data and design matrix
  
  Y <- as.numeric(data[[response]])   

  X <- model.matrix(
    reformulate(covariates, response = NULL),  # create design matrix with intercept
    data = data
  )

  coords <- as.matrix(coords)

  n <- length(Y)
  p <- ncol(X)

  if (nrow(X) != n || nrow(coords) != n) {
    stop("Y, X and coordinates must have the same number of rows.")
  }

  if (!all(is.finite(Y))) {
    stop("The response contains NA, NaN or Inf.")
  }

  if (!all(is.finite(X))) {
    stop("The design matrix contains NA, NaN or Inf.")
  }

  if (!all(is.finite(coords))) {
    stop("The coordinates contain NA, NaN or Inf.")
  }

  if (n_iter < 2 || burnin < 0 || burnin >= n_iter || thin < 1) {
    stop("Require n_iter >= 2, 0 <= burnin < n_iter, and thin >= 1.")
  }

  if (!is.finite(phi_proposal_sd) || phi_proposal_sd <= 0) {
    stop("phi_proposal_sd must be positive and finite.")
  }

  # Standardising coordinates makes phi dimensionless. The transformation
  # attributes are retained for interpretation and future prediction.
  coords_scaled <- scale(coords)
  coord_center <- attr(coords_scaled, "scaled:center") # This extracts the means used for centering:
  coord_scale <- attr(coords_scaled, "scaled:scale") # This extracts the standard deviations used for scaling:
  
  
  distance_matrix <- as.matrix(dist(coords_scaled)) # We will use the distance matrix for the below function.

  #  Spatial correlation matrix
  make_correlation <- function(phi) {
    if (!is.finite(phi) || phi <= 0) {
      stop("phi must be positive and finite.")
    }

    if (cov_family == "exponential") {
      R <- exp(-distance_matrix / phi)
    } else if (cov_family == "matern") {
      R <- geoR::matern(
        distance_matrix,
        phi = phi,
        kappa = 1.5
      )
    } else {
      stop("Use cov_family = 'exponential' or 'matern'.")
    }

    # A tiny diagonal jitter protects Cholesky decompositions from rounding
    # problems 
    # It is not the nugget variance tau2-it's purely a computational trick
    R + diag(1e-8, n)
  }

  
  # important helper function.
  # Draw N(Q^{-1}b, Q^{-1}) using the Cholesky factor of precision Q.
  rmvn_precision <- function(precision, linear_term) {
    U <- chol(precision)

    posterior_mean <- backsolve(
      U,
      forwardsolve(t(U), linear_term)
    )

    random_part <- backsolve(U, rnorm(length(linear_term)))

    as.numeric(posterior_mean + random_part)
  }
  
  

  # Initial values
  beta_current <- if (is.null(initial_values$beta)) {
    as.numeric(qr.solve(X, Y)) # use QR decomposition to solve linear equation for beta
  } else {
    as.numeric(initial_values$beta)
  }
  

  if (length(beta_current) != p || !all(is.finite(beta_current))) {
    stop("initial_values$beta must contain ", p, " finite values.")
  }

  W_current <- if (is.null(initial_values$W)) { # our default initial value of W is Null,
    rep(0, n)
  } else {
    as.numeric(initial_values$W)
  }

  if (length(W_current) != n || !all(is.finite(W_current))) {
    stop("initial_values$W must contain ", n, " finite values.")
  }

  # use our defualt values
  sigma2_current <- initial_values$sigma2
  tau2_current <- initial_values$tau2
  phi_current <- initial_values$phi
  
  
  

  positive_initials <- c(
    sigma2 = sigma2_current,
    tau2 = tau2_current,
    phi = phi_current
  )

  if (!all(is.finite(positive_initials)) || any(positive_initials <= 0)) {
    stop("Initial sigma2, tau2 and phi must be positive and finite.")
  }

  
  beta_prior_mean <- rep(priors$beta_mean, p)
  beta_prior_precision <- diag(1 / priors$beta_var, p) # check the default value of the fuction.

  # Allocate storage
  beta_chain <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_iter, ncol = p)
  
  W_chain <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_iter, ncol = n)
  
  sigma2_chain <- numeric(n_iter)
  
  tau2_chain <- numeric(n_iter)
  
  phi_chain <- numeric(n_iter)
  
  log_likelihood_chain <- numeric(n_iter)
  
  phi_accepted <- logical(n_iter)  # default as FALSE

  beta_chain[1, ] <- beta_current
  W_chain[1, ] <- W_current
  sigma2_chain[1] <- sigma2_current
  tau2_chain[1] <- tau2_current
  phi_chain[1] <- phi_current

  R_current <- make_correlation(phi_current)  #correlation matrix R, exponential or Matern with parameter phi.
  
  Sigma_Y <- sigma2_current * R_current + tau2_current * diag(n)  ### Total covariance = spatial covariance + nugget covariance, see math explanation
  
    log_likelihood_chain[1] <- mvtnorm::dmvnorm(  #PDF of multivariate normal distribution
    Y,
    mean = as.numeric(X %*% beta_current),
    sigma = Sigma_Y,
    log = TRUE
  )

  cat("\nRunning MCMC for", cov_family, "covariance function...\n")
  cat("Number of observations:", n, "\n")
  cat("Number of regression coefficients:", p, "\n")

  #  MCMC iterations
  for (i in 2:n_iter) {
    
    if (progress_every > 0 && i %% progress_every == 0) {  cat("Iteration:", i, "\n")   }

    # beta | Y, W, tau2
    beta_precision <-
      crossprod(X) / tau2_current + beta_prior_precision

    beta_linear_term <-
      crossprod(X, Y - W_current) / tau2_current +
      beta_prior_precision %*% beta_prior_mean

    beta_current <- rmvn_precision(
      beta_precision,
      beta_linear_term
    )

    # W | Y, beta, sigma2, tau2, phi
    R_current <- make_correlation(phi_current)
    R_inverse <- chol2inv(chol(R_current))

    W_precision <-
      diag(1 / tau2_current, n) + R_inverse / sigma2_current

    W_linear_term <-
      as.numeric(Y - X %*% beta_current) / tau2_current

    W_current <- rmvn_precision(W_precision, W_linear_term)

    # sigma2 | W, phi
    sigma2_shape <- priors$sigma2_shape + n / 2
    sigma2_rate <- priors$sigma2_rate +
      0.5 * drop(crossprod(W_current, R_inverse %*% W_current))

    sigma2_current <- 1 / rgamma(
      1,
      shape = sigma2_shape,
      rate = sigma2_rate
    )

    # tau2 | Y, beta, W
    residual <- as.numeric(Y - X %*% beta_current - W_current)
    tau2_shape <- priors$tau2_shape + n / 2
    tau2_rate <- priors$tau2_rate + 0.5 * sum(residual^2)

    tau2_current <- 1 / rgamma(
      1,
      shape = tau2_shape,
      rate = tau2_rate
    )

    # phi | W, sigma2: random-walk MH on eta = log(phi).
    # The +eta terms are the Jacobians for transforming phi to log(phi).
    # Save the current state so rejection can be shown explicitly.
    phi_old <- phi_current
    R_old <- R_current

    eta_current <- log(phi_current)
    eta_proposed <- rnorm(1, eta_current, phi_proposal_sd)
    phi_proposed <- exp(eta_proposed)
    R_proposed <- make_correlation(phi_proposed)

    log_target_current <- mvtnorm::dmvnorm(
      W_current,
      mean = rep(0, n),
      sigma = sigma2_current * R_current,
      log = TRUE
    ) +
      dgamma(
        phi_current,
        shape = priors$phi_shape,
        rate = priors$phi_rate,
        log = TRUE
      ) +
      eta_current

    log_target_proposed <- mvtnorm::dmvnorm(
      W_current,
      mean = rep(0, n),
      sigma = sigma2_current * R_proposed,
      log = TRUE
    ) +
      dgamma(
        phi_proposed,
        shape = priors$phi_shape,
        rate = priors$phi_rate,
        log = TRUE
      ) +
      eta_proposed

    log_acceptance_ratio <- log_target_proposed - log_target_current

    if (
      is.finite(log_acceptance_ratio) &&
      log(runif(1)) < log_acceptance_ratio
    ) {
      # Accept: move the chain to the proposed state.
      phi_current <- phi_proposed
      R_current <- R_proposed
      phi_accepted[i] <- TRUE
    } else {
      # Reject: repeat the previous state in the Markov chain.
      phi_current <- phi_old
      R_current <- R_old
      phi_accepted[i] <- FALSE
    }

    # Marginal likelihood Y | beta, sigma2, tau2, phi
    Sigma_Y <- sigma2_current * R_current + tau2_current * diag(n)  ## Total covariance = spatial covariance + nugget covariance

    log_likelihood_current <- mvtnorm::dmvnorm(  # PDF of multiviate normal distribution
      Y,
      mean = as.numeric(X %*% beta_current),
      sigma = Sigma_Y,
      log = TRUE
    )

    current_values <- c(
      beta_current,
      W_current,
      sigma2_current,
      tau2_current,
      phi_current,
      log_likelihood_current
    )

    if (!all(is.finite(current_values))) {
      stop("A non-finite value was generated at iteration ", i, ".")
    }

    beta_chain[i, ] <- beta_current
    W_chain[i, ] <- W_current
    sigma2_chain[i] <- sigma2_current
    tau2_chain[i] <- tau2_current
    phi_chain[i] <- phi_current
    log_likelihood_chain[i] <- log_likelihood_current
  }

  # Burn-in and thinning
  keep_idx <- seq(burnin + 1, n_iter, by = thin)

  mcmc_samples <- cbind(
    beta_chain[keep_idx, , drop = FALSE],
    sigma2 = sigma2_chain[keep_idx],
    tau2 = tau2_chain[keep_idx],
    phi = phi_chain[keep_idx],
    log_lik = log_likelihood_chain[keep_idx]
  )

  colnames(mcmc_samples)[seq_len(p)] <- paste0("beta_", 0:(p - 1))

  if (!all(is.finite(mcmc_samples))) {
    bad_values <- which(!is.finite(mcmc_samples), arr.ind = TRUE)
    print(bad_values)
    stop("Non-finite values were found in retained MCMC samples.")
  }

  mcmc_object <- coda::mcmc(
    mcmc_samples,
    start = burnin + 1,
    thin = thin
  )

  list(
    samples = mcmc_object,
    parameters = list(
      beta = beta_chain[keep_idx, , drop = FALSE],
      W = W_chain[keep_idx, , drop = FALSE],
      sigma2 = sigma2_chain[keep_idx],
      tau2 = tau2_chain[keep_idx],
      phi = phi_chain[keep_idx],
      log_likelihood = log_likelihood_chain[keep_idx]
    ),
    acceptance_rate = mean(phi_accepted[2:n_iter]),
    kept_iterations = keep_idx,
    coordinate_scaling = list(
      center = coord_center,
      scale = coord_scale
    ),
    settings = list(
      n_iter = n_iter,
      burnin = burnin,
      thin = thin,
      cov_family = cov_family,
      phi_proposal_sd = phi_proposal_sd
    )
  )
}



```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
Sigma_Y <- sigma2_current * R_current + tau2_current * diag(n)
```

## 8.1 math behind the above R code for covariance of Y

### 8.1.1 The Statistical Model

#### Model Specification

Recall the spatial linear model:

$$\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{W} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon},$$

where:

- $\mathbf{Y}$: $n \times 1$ response vector
- $\mathbf{X}$: $n \times p$ design matrix
- $\boldsymbol{\beta}$: $p \times 1$ vector of regression coefficients
- $\mathbf{W}$: $n \times 1$ vector of spatial random effects
- $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$: $n \times 1$ vector of independent errors (nugget)

#### Variance-Covariance Structure

The total variance of $\mathbf{Y}$, conditional on $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, is:

$$\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{Y})
= \operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{W})
+ \operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}),$$

because $\mathbf{W}$ and $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ are independent.

#### Components of the Covariance Matrix

##### Component 1: Spatial Variance $\sigma^2\mathbf{R}$

The spatial random effects have covariance:

$$\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{W})
= \sigma^2\mathbf{R}(\phi),$$

where:

- $\sigma^2$: spatial variance parameter (partial sill)
- $\mathbf{R}(\phi)$: spatial correlation matrix that depends on $\phi$

#### Component 2: Nugget Variance $\tau^2\mathbf{I}$

The independent errors have covariance:

$$\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})
= \tau^2\mathbf{I},$$

where:

- $\tau^2$: nugget variance
- $\mathbf{I}$: $n \times n$ identity matrix

#### Total Covariance

Therefore,

$$\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{Y})
= \sigma^2\mathbf{R}(\phi) + \tau^2\mathbf{I}.$$

```{r, eval=FALSE}
log_likelihood_current <- dmvnorm(
    Y,
    mean = as.numeric(X %*% beta_current),
    sigma = Sigma_Y,
    log = TRUE
)
```

The above R code calculate the The multivariate normal log-likelihood :

$$\log L = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi)
          - \frac{1}{2}\log|\Sigma|
          - \frac{1}{2}(Y-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1}(Y-\mu)$$

Where:

$$\mu = X\beta$$

and

$$\Sigma = \sigma^2 R + \tau^2 I$$

# 9 Mathematics of How $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ Was Updated


# Model specification

The spatial linear model is

$$
\mathbf{Y}
=
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
+
\mathbf{W}
+
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},
$$

where:

- $\mathbf{Y}$ is an $n \times 1$ vector of responses;
- $\mathbf{X}$ is an $n \times p$ design matrix;
- $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is a $p \times 1$ vector of regression coefficients;
- $\mathbf{W}$ is an $n \times 1$ vector of spatial random effects; and
- $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ is an $n \times 1$ vector of independent errors.

## Distributional assumptions

The model assumes

$$
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
\sim
N_n\left(\mathbf{0},\tau^2\mathbf{I}_n\right)
$$

and

$$
\mathbf{W}
\sim
N_n\left\{\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{R}(\phi)\right\}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\mathbf{Y}
\mid
\boldsymbol{\beta},\mathbf{W},\tau^2
\sim
N_n\left(
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{W},
\tau^2\mathbf{I}_n
\right).
$$

## Prior specification

The prior for $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is multivariate normal:

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta}
\sim
N_p\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_0,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0\right),
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\mu}_0$ is the prior mean vector and
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0$ is the prior covariance matrix.

# Part 1: The likelihood function

## Step 1: Rewrite the model in terms of the errors

From

$$
\mathbf{Y}
=
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
+
\mathbf{W}
+
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},
$$

we obtain

$$
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
=
\mathbf{Y}
-
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
-
\mathbf{W}.
$$

## Step 2: Write the density of the errors

Since
$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\sim
N_n(\mathbf{0},\tau^2\mathbf{I}_n)$,
its probability density function is

$$
f(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})
=
\frac{1}
{(2\pi)^{n/2}\lvert\tau^2\mathbf{I}_n\rvert^{1/2}}
\exp\left\{
  -\frac{1}{2}
  \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{\mathsf T}
  (\tau^2\mathbf{I}_n)^{-1}
  \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
\right\}.
$$

## Step 3: Simplify the density

The determinant is

$$
\lvert\tau^2\mathbf{I}_n\rvert^{1/2}
=
(\tau^{2n})^{1/2}
=
\tau^n,
$$

and the inverse is

$$
(\tau^2\mathbf{I}_n)^{-1}
=
\frac{1}{\tau^2}\mathbf{I}_n.
$$

Therefore,

$$
f(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})
=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\tau^n}
\exp\left\{
  -\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
  \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{\mathsf T}
  \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
\right\}.
$$

## Step 4: Substitute the expression for the errors

Substituting
$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
=\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathbf{W}$
gives

$$
f(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})
=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\tau^n}
\exp\left\{
  -\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
  (\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathbf{W})^{\mathsf T}
  (\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathbf{W})
\right\}.
$$

## Step 5: Transform from the errors to the response

The likelihood of $\mathbf{Y}$ is

$$
L(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{W},\tau^2)
=
f_{\mathbf{Y}}
(\mathbf{Y}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\mathbf{W},\tau^2).
$$

Because

$$
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
=
\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathbf{W}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}{\partial\mathbf{Y}}
=
\mathbf{I}_n,
$$

the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant is one. Thus,

$$
f_{\mathbf{Y}}
(\mathbf{Y}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\mathbf{W},\tau^2)
=
f_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}
(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathbf{W}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
f(\mathbf{Y}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\mathbf{W},\tau^2)
=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\tau^n}
\exp\left\{
  -\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
  (\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathbf{W})^{\mathsf T}
  (\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathbf{W})
\right\}.
$$

## Step 6: The likelihood as a function of the regression coefficients

Viewed as a function of $\boldsymbol{\beta}$,

$$
L(\boldsymbol{\beta})
=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\tau^n}
\exp\left\{
  -\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
  (\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathbf{W})^{\mathsf T}
  (\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathbf{W})
\right\}.
$$

## Step 7: The likelihood up to proportionality

When deriving the full conditional distribution, terms that do not depend on
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ can be omitted:

$$
L(\boldsymbol{\beta})
\propto
\exp\left\{
  -\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
  (\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathbf{W})^{\mathsf T}
  (\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathbf{W})
\right\}.
$$

The normalising constant is dropped because it does not contain
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$, cancels in ratios, and does not affect the shape of the
conditional distribution.

# Part 2: The full conditional distribution of $\boldsymbol{\beta}$

## Step 1: Expand the likelihood

The quadratic form can be expanded as

$$
\begin{aligned}
&(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\mathsf T}
(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\\
&\quad=
(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})
-2\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}
(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})
+\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}.
\end{aligned}
$$

After removing terms that are constant with respect to
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$,

$$
L(\boldsymbol{\beta})
\propto
\exp\left\{
  -\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
  \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}
  \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
  +\frac{1}{\tau^2}
  \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}
  (\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})
\right\}.
$$

## Step 2: Write and expand the prior

The prior density, up to proportionality, is

$$
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})
\propto
\exp\left\{
  -\frac{1}{2}
  (\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_0)^{\mathsf T}
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
  (\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_0)
\right\}.
$$

The quadratic form is

$$
\begin{aligned}
&(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_0)^{\mathsf T}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_0)\\
&\quad=
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
\boldsymbol{\beta}
-2\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
\boldsymbol{\mu}_0
+\boldsymbol{\mu}_0^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
\boldsymbol{\mu}_0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})
\propto
\exp\left\{
  -\frac{1}{2}
  \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
  \boldsymbol{\beta}
  +\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_0
\right\}.
$$

## Step 3: Combine the likelihood and prior

By Bayes' theorem,

$$
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{W},\tau^2)
\propto
L(\boldsymbol{\beta})\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta}).
$$

Taking logarithms and omitting additive constants gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{W},\tau^2)
={}&
-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
+\frac{1}{\tau^2}
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}
(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})\\
&-\frac{1}{2}
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
\boldsymbol{\beta}
+\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
\boldsymbol{\mu}_0
+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 4: Collect terms in $\boldsymbol{\beta}$

Collecting the quadratic and linear terms yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{W},\tau^2)
={}&
-\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}
\left(
  \frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}}{\tau^2}
  +\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
\right)
\boldsymbol{\beta}\\
&+
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}
\left[
  \frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})}{\tau^2}
  +\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0
\right]
+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

Define the posterior precision matrix and linear term as

$$
\mathbf{Q}_{\beta}
=
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}}{\tau^2}
+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
$$

and

$$
\mathbf{b}_{\beta}
=
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})}{\tau^2}
+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0.
$$

Then

$$
\log\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\cdot)
=
-\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}
\mathbf{Q}_{\beta}\boldsymbol{\beta}
+\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{b}_{\beta}
+C.
$$

## Step 5: Recognise the multivariate normal form

For

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta}
\sim
N_p(\boldsymbol{\mu}_*,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*),
$$

the log-density can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})
&=
-\frac{1}{2}
(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_*)^{\mathsf T}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*^{-1}
(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_*)
+C\\
&=
-\frac{1}{2}
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*^{-1}
\boldsymbol{\beta}
+\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf T}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_*
+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 6: Match coefficients

Matching the quadratic terms gives

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*^{-1}
=
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}}{\tau^2}
+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
=
\mathbf{Q}_{\beta}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*
=
\mathbf{Q}_{\beta}^{-1}.
$$

Matching the linear terms gives

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_*
=
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})}{\tau^2}
+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0
=
\mathbf{b}_{\beta}.
$$

Thus,

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_*
=
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*
\left[
  \frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})}{\tau^2}
  +\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0
\right]
=
\mathbf{Q}_{\beta}^{-1}\mathbf{b}_{\beta}.
$$

## Step 7: Final result

The full conditional distribution is

$$
\boxed{
\boldsymbol{\beta}
\mid
\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{W},\tau^2
\sim
N_p(\boldsymbol{\mu}_*,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*)
}
$$

where

$$
\boxed{
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*^{-1}
=
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}}{\tau^2}
+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\boldsymbol{\mu}_*
=
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*
\left[
  \frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})}{\tau^2}
  +\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0
\right].
}
$$

# Part 3: Connection to the R code

## R implementation

The full conditional distribution is implemented in the MCMC function as
follows:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Posterior precision matrix
beta_precision <- crossprod(X) / tau2_current +
  beta_prior_precision

# Linear term
beta_linear_term <- crossprod(X, Y - W_current) / tau2_current +
  beta_prior_precision %*% beta_prior_mean

# Draw from the multivariate normal full conditional distribution
beta_current <- rmvn_precision(
  beta_precision,
  beta_linear_term
)
```

The mathematical equivalents are

$$
\mathtt{\beta\_precision}
=
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}}{\tau^2}
+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1},
$$

$$
\mathtt{\beta\_linear\_term}
=
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})}{\tau^2}
+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0,
$$

and

$$
\mathtt{\beta\_current}
\sim
N_p\left(
\mathtt{\beta\_precision}^{-1}*
\mathtt{\beta\_linear\_term}, \text{  } 
\mathtt{\beta\_precision}^{-1}
\right).
$$

## The `rmvn_precision()` function

```{r, eval=FALSE}
rmvn_precision <- function(precision, linear_term) {
  U <- chol(precision)

  posterior_mean <- backsolve(
    U,
    forwardsolve(t(U), linear_term)
  )

  random_part <- backsolve(
    U,
    rnorm(length(linear_term))
  )

  as.numeric(posterior_mean + random_part)
}
```

This function:

1. computes the upper-triangular Cholesky factor
   $\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{U}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{U}$;
2. solves for the posterior mean
   $\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$;
3. generates $\mathbf{z}\sim N_p(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_p)$; and
4. returns

$$
\mathbf{x}
=
\boldsymbol{\mu}
+
\mathbf{U}^{-1}\mathbf{z}.
$$

Because
$\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{U}^{-1}\mathbf{z})
=\mathbf{U}^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{-\mathsf T}
=\mathbf{Q}^{-1}$,
the returned value has distribution

$$
\mathbf{x}
\sim
N_p(\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{b},\mathbf{Q}^{-1}).
$$

# Part 4: Special cases

## Case 1: Flat prior

When $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\rightarrow\mathbf{0}$,

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*^{-1}
=
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}}{\tau^2}
$$

and

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_*
=
(\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W}).
$$

This is the ordinary least-squares estimate of $\boldsymbol{\beta}$,
conditional on $\mathbf{W}$.

## Case 2: Ridge prior

If
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}=\lambda\mathbf{I}_p$
and $\boldsymbol{\mu}_0=\mathbf{0}$, then

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*^{-1}
=
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}}{\tau^2}
+\lambda\mathbf{I}_p
$$

and

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_*
=
\left(
  \frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}}{\tau^2}
  +\lambda\mathbf{I}_p
\right)^{-1}
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})}{\tau^2}.
$$

This is the ridge-regression posterior mean, conditional on $\mathbf{W}$.

## Case 3: No spatial effect

When $\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{0}$,

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_*
=
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*
\left(
  \frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{Y}}{\tau^2}
  +\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0
\right),
$$

which is the posterior mean from standard Bayesian linear regression.

# Part 5: Intuitive interpretation

The posterior precision is the sum of the information contributed by the data
and the prior:

$$
\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*^{-1}}_{\text{posterior precision}}
=
\underbrace{\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X}}{\tau^2}}
_{\text{data precision}}
+
\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}}
_{\text{prior precision}}.
$$

The posterior information vector is similarly

$$
\underbrace{\mathbf{b}_{\beta}}_{\text{posterior information}}
=
\underbrace{
\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W})}{\tau^2}
}_{\text{data information}}
+
\underbrace{
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0
}_{\text{prior information}}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_*
=
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_*\mathbf{b}_{\beta}.
$$

The main insights are:

- The data contribution uses $\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{W}$, the response after removing the current spatial effect.
- The prior contribution pulls the posterior toward   $\boldsymbol{\mu}_0$.
- A smaller nugget variance $\tau^2$ gives more weight to the data.
- As $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\rightarrow\mathbf{0}$, the posterior mean approaches the ordinary least-squares solution conditional on $\mathbf{W}$.


# 10 Mathematics of How $W$ Was Updated


## 10.1 Model specification

The spatial linear model is

$$
\mathbf Y = \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta + \mathbf W + \boldsymbol\varepsilon,
$$

where:

- $\mathbf Y$ is an $n \times 1$ vector of responses;
- $\mathbf X$ is an $n \times p$ design matrix;
- $\boldsymbol\beta$ is a $p \times 1$ vector of regression coefficients;
- $\mathbf W$ is an $n \times 1$ vector of spatial random effects; and
- $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ is an $n \times 1$ vector of independent errors.

## 10.2 Distributional assumptions

The model assumes

$$
\boldsymbol\varepsilon \sim N_n(\mathbf 0,\tau^2\mathbf I_n)
$$

and

$$
\mathbf W \sim N_n\left\{\mathbf 0,\sigma^2\mathbf R(\phi)\right\}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\mathbf Y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W,\tau^2
\sim
N_n\left(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\mathbf W,\tau^2\mathbf I_n\right).
$$

## 10.3 The likelihood function for $\mathbf W$

### 10.3.1 Rewrite the model in terms of errors

From the model, we solve for the errors:

$$
\boldsymbol\varepsilon
=\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W.
$$

### 10.3.2 Write the density of the errors

Since $\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim N_n(\mathbf 0,\tau^2\mathbf I_n)$, its probability density is

$$
f(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}|\tau^2\mathbf I_n|^{1/2}}
\exp\left\{-\frac12
\boldsymbol\varepsilon^\mathsf T
(\tau^2\mathbf I_n)^{-1}
\boldsymbol\varepsilon\right\}.
$$

### 10.3.3 Simplify the density

The determinant is

$$
|\tau^2\mathbf I_n|^{1/2}
=(\tau^{2n})^{1/2}=\tau^n,
$$

and the inverse is

$$
(\tau^2\mathbf I_n)^{-1}=\frac{1}{\tau^2}\mathbf I_n.
$$

Thus,

$$
f(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\tau^n}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
\boldsymbol\varepsilon^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\varepsilon\right\}.
$$

### 10.3.4 Substitute the expression for $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$

Substitution gives

$$
f(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\tau^n}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)^\mathsf T
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)\right\}.
$$

### 10.3.5 Transform from errors to $\mathbf Y$

Because

$$
\boldsymbol\varepsilon=\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W
\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac{\partial\boldsymbol\varepsilon}{\partial\mathbf Y}=\mathbf I_n,
$$

the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant is 1. Therefore,

$$
f(\mathbf Y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W,\tau^2)
=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\tau^n}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)^\mathsf T
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)\right\}.
$$

### 10.3.6 View the likelihood as a function of $\mathbf W$

Holding $\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\tau^2$ fixed,

$$
L(\mathbf W)
=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\tau^n}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)^\mathsf T
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)\right\}.
$$

Up to a constant that does not depend on $\mathbf W$,

$$
L(\mathbf W)\propto
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)^\mathsf T
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)\right\}.
$$

The factor $1/\{(2\pi)^{n/2}\tau^n\}$ can be dropped because it does not contain $\mathbf W$, cancels in ratios, and does not affect the shape of the conditional distribution.

### 10.3.7 Expand the likelihood

Let $\mathbf r=\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$. Then

$$
(\mathbf r-\mathbf W)^\mathsf T(\mathbf r-\mathbf W)
=\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r
-2\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf r
+\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf W.
$$

After dropping the term $\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r$, which does not depend on $\mathbf W$,

$$
L(\mathbf W)\propto
\exp\left\{
-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf W
+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\mathbf W^\mathsf T
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
\right\}.
$$

## 10.4 The full conditional distribution for $\mathbf W$

### 10.4.1 Prior for $\mathbf W$

Ignoring its normalising constant, the prior density is

$$
\pi(\mathbf W)\propto
\exp\left\{-\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T
(\sigma^2\mathbf R)^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}.
$$

Because

$$
(\sigma^2\mathbf R)^{-1}=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\mathbf R^{-1},
$$

we have

$$
\pi(\mathbf W)\propto
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}.
$$

### 10.4.2 Combine the likelihood and prior

By Bayes' theorem,

$$
\pi(\mathbf W\mid\mathbf Y,\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2,\phi)
\propto L(\mathbf W)\pi(\mathbf W).
$$

Taking logarithms and ignoring constants,

$$
\log\pi(\mathbf W\mid\cdot)
=-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf W
+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\mathbf W^\mathsf T
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W.
$$

Collecting terms in $\mathbf W$ gives

$$
\log\pi(\mathbf W\mid\cdot)
=-\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T
\underbrace{\left(
\frac{1}{\tau^2}\mathbf I_n+
\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\mathbf R^{-1}
\right)}_{\text{posterior precision}}
\mathbf W
+\mathbf W^\mathsf T
\underbrace{\left\{
\frac{1}{\tau^2}(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
\right\}}_{\text{linear term}}.
$$

### 10.4.3 Recognise the multivariate normal form

For $\mathbf W\sim N_n(\boldsymbol\mu_W^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*)$, the log density is

$$
\log\pi(\mathbf W)
=-\frac12
(\mathbf W-\boldsymbol\mu_W^*)^\mathsf T
(\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*)^{-1}
(\mathbf W-\boldsymbol\mu_W^*)+\text{constant}.
$$

Expanding it gives

$$
\log\pi(\mathbf W)
=-\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T
(\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*)^{-1}\mathbf W
+\mathbf W^\mathsf T
(\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*)^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_W^*
+\text{constant}.
$$

Matching the quadratic terms yields

$$
(\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*)^{-1}
=\frac{1}{\tau^2}\mathbf I_n
+\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\mathbf R^{-1}.
$$

Matching the linear terms yields

$$
(\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*)^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_W^*
=\frac{1}{\tau^2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta),
$$

and hence

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_W^*
=\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*
\left\{\frac{1}{\tau^2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)\right\}.
$$

### 10.4.4 Final result

The full conditional distribution is

$$
\mathbf W\mid\mathbf Y,\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2,\phi
\sim N_n(\boldsymbol\mu_W^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*),
$$

where

$$
(\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*)^{-1}
=\frac{1}{\tau^2}\mathbf I_n
+\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\mathbf R^{-1}
$$

and

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_W^*
=\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*
\left\{\frac{1}{\tau^2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)\right\}.
$$

## 10.5 Alternative derivation using the joint distribution

From the model,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf Y\\
\mathbf W
\end{pmatrix}
\sim
N_{2n}\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\\
\mathbf 0
\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau^2\mathbf I_n+\sigma^2\mathbf R & \sigma^2\mathbf R\\
\sigma^2\mathbf R & \sigma^2\mathbf R
\end{pmatrix}
\right\}.
$$

The conditional normal formula gives

$$
\mathbf W\mid\mathbf Y
\sim N_n(\boldsymbol\mu_{W\mid Y},\boldsymbol\Sigma_{W\mid Y}),
$$

where

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_{W\mid Y}
=\sigma^2\mathbf R
(\tau^2\mathbf I_n+\sigma^2\mathbf R)^{-1}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
$$

and

$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma_{W\mid Y}
=\sigma^2\mathbf R
-\sigma^2\mathbf R
(\tau^2\mathbf I_n+\sigma^2\mathbf R)^{-1}
\sigma^2\mathbf R.
$$

This is equivalent to the precision-based formulation.

## 10.6 Connection to the R code

The conditional distribution is implemented in the MCMC function as follows:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Compute R^{-1} using Cholesky decomposition
R_current <- make_correlation(phi_current)
R_inverse <- chol2inv(chol(R_current))

# Build the precision matrix and linear term
W_precision <- diag(1 / tau2_current, n) +
  R_inverse / sigma2_current

W_linear_term <- as.numeric(Y - X %*% beta_current) /
  tau2_current

# Sample from the multivariate normal distribution
W_current <- rmvn_precision(W_precision, W_linear_term)
```

The mathematical equivalents are

$$
\mathtt{W\_precision}
=\frac{1}{\tau^2}\mathbf I_n
+\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\mathbf R^{-1},
$$

$$
\mathtt{W\_linear\_term}
=\frac{1}{\tau^2}(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta),
$$

and

$$
\mathtt{W\_current}
\sim N_n\left(
\mathtt{W\_precision}^{-1}\mathtt{W\_linear\_term},
\mathtt{W\_precision}^{-1}
\right).
$$

## 10.7 The `rmvn_precision()` function

```{r, eval=FALSE}
rmvn_precision <- function(precision, linear_term) {
  U <- chol(precision)

  posterior_mean <- backsolve(
    U,
    forwardsolve(t(U), linear_term)
  )

  random_part <- backsolve(
    U,
    rnorm(length(linear_term))
  )

  as.numeric(posterior_mean + random_part)
}
```

This function:

1. computes the Cholesky factor $\mathbf Q=\mathbf U^\mathsf T\mathbf U$;
2. solves for the mean $\boldsymbol\mu=\mathbf Q^{-1}\mathbf b$;
3. generates $\mathbf z\sim N_n(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I_n)$; and
4. returns $\mathbf x=\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf U^{-1}\mathbf z$.

## 10.8 Computing $\mathbf R^{-1}$ using Cholesky decomposition

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Step 1: Compute the Cholesky factor of R
U <- chol(R_current)

# Step 2: Compute R^{-1}
R_inverse <- chol2inv(U)
```

The Cholesky decomposition is

$$
\mathbf R=\mathbf U^\mathsf T\mathbf U,
$$

where $\mathbf U$ is upper triangular. Therefore,

$$
\mathbf R^{-1}
=\mathbf U^{-1}\mathbf U^{-\mathsf T}
=\mathbf U^{-1}(\mathbf U^\mathsf T)^{-1}.
$$

The `chol2inv()` function obtains this inverse using triangular-system calculations.

### 10.8.1 Intuitive interpretation of Precision matrix

$$
(\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*)^{-1}
=\frac{1}{\tau^2}\mathbf I_n
+\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\mathbf R^{-1}.
$$

| Term | Source | Interpretation |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $\mathbf I_n/\tau^2$ | Data (likelihood) | Information from the residuals |
| $\mathbf R^{-1}/\sigma^2$ | Prior (process) | Spatial smoothness constraint |

## 10.9 Mean vector

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_W^*
=\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*
\left\{\frac{1}{\tau^2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)\right\}.
$$

This is a shrinkage estimator. It pulls $\mathbf W$ toward the residuals $\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$, while smoothing them using the spatial correlation structure. The amount of shrinkage depends on $\sigma^2$, $\tau^2$, and $\phi$.

## 10.10 Relationship to kriging

The conditional mean of $\mathbf W$ is the best linear predictor:

$$
\widehat{\mathbf W}
=\sigma^2\mathbf R
(\tau^2\mathbf I_n+\sigma^2\mathbf R)^{-1}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta).
$$

This is equivalent to the kriging predictor in geostatistics when the model parameters are known.

## 10.11 Special cases

## No spatial variation: $\sigma^2\to 0$

As the spatial variance approaches zero,

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_W^*\to\mathbf 0,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*\to\mathbf 0.
$$

Thus, the spatial random effects shrink toward zero.

## 10.12 Vanishing nugget variance: $\tau^2\to 0$

As the independent-error variance approaches zero,

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_W^*
\to\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*\to\mathbf 0.
$$

Thus, $\mathbf W$ is forced toward the residual vector.

## 10.13 Known $\boldsymbol\beta$

When $\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$ is fixed,

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_W^*
=\boldsymbol\Sigma_W^*
\left\{\frac{1}{\tau^2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)\right\},
$$

which is the standard spatial prediction expression with a known mean.


## 10.14 Note for update $\beta$ and $W$


Both $\beta$ and $W$ are updated using Gibbs sampling because:

- Their full conditional distributions are multivariate normal

- These distributions have closed forms

- They can be sampled from directly using rmvn_precision()

- Every sample is accepted (no rejection)

- No tuning is required


# 11 Mathematics of How $\sigma^2$ Was Updated

## 11.1 The model and assumptions

### 11.1.1 Process model: prior for $\mathbf W$

$$
\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi
\sim
N_n\left\{\mathbf 0,\sigma^2\mathbf R(\phi)\right\}.
$$

### 11.1.2 Prior for $\sigma^2$

Assume

$$
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{IG}(a_\sigma,b_\sigma),
$$

using the shape--scale form of the Inverse-Gamma distribution. Its density is

$$
\pi(\sigma^2)
=
\frac{b_\sigma^{a_\sigma}}{\Gamma(a_\sigma)}
(\sigma^2)^{-a_\sigma-1}
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\sigma}{\sigma^2}\right),
\qquad \sigma^2>0,
$$

where:

- $a_\sigma$ is the shape parameter; and
- $b_\sigma$ is the scale parameter in this Inverse-Gamma parameterisation.

> **Parameterisation note:** In the density above, $b_\sigma$ appears in the numerator of $b_\sigma/\sigma^2$. It is therefore conventionally called the Inverse-Gamma **scale** parameter. Equivalently, if $1/\sigma^2$ is Gamma distributed, $b_\sigma$ is its Gamma rate parameter.

## 11.2 The prior density for $\mathbf W$

### 11.2.1 Full expression

From

$$
\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi
\sim N_n(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2\mathbf R),
$$

the density is

$$
f(\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi)
=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}|\sigma^2\mathbf R|^{1/2}}
\exp\left\{
-\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T
(\sigma^2\mathbf R)^{-1}\mathbf W
\right\}.
$$

- Simplify the determinant

Because $\mathbf R$ is an $n\times n$ matrix,

$$
|\sigma^2\mathbf R|^{1/2}
=\left\{(\sigma^2)^n|\mathbf R|\right\}^{1/2}
=(\sigma^2)^{n/2}|\mathbf R|^{1/2}
=\sigma^n|\mathbf R|^{1/2}.
$$

- Simplify the inverse

$$
(\sigma^2\mathbf R)^{-1}
=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\mathbf R^{-1}.
$$
- Substitute

Therefore,

$$
f(\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi)
=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}(\sigma^2)^{n/2}|\mathbf R|^{1/2}}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W
\right\}.
$$

## 11.3 The prior for $\sigma^2$

The Inverse-Gamma prior is

$$
\pi(\sigma^2)
=
\frac{b_\sigma^{a_\sigma}}{\Gamma(a_\sigma)}
(\sigma^2)^{-a_\sigma-1}
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\sigma}{\sigma^2}\right).
$$

In general, if

$$
X\sim\operatorname{IG}(\alpha,\beta),
$$

then

$$
f(x)
=
\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}
x^{-\alpha-1}
\exp\left(-\frac{\beta}{x}\right),
\qquad x>0.
$$

Thus, in the present notation,

$$
\alpha=a_\sigma,
\qquad
\beta=b_\sigma.
$$

## 11.4 Combine the density of $\mathbf W$ and the prior for $\sigma^2$

By Bayes' theorem,

$$
\pi(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf W,\phi)
\propto
f(\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi)\,
\pi(\sigma^2).
$$

## 11.5 Write the unnormalised posterior

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf W,\phi)
&\propto
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}(\sigma^2)^{n/2}|\mathbf R|^{1/2}}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}\\
&\quad\times
\frac{b_\sigma^{a_\sigma}}{\Gamma(a_\sigma)}
(\sigma^2)^{-a_\sigma-1}
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\sigma}{\sigma^2}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

- Drop constants not involving $\sigma^2$

The following terms do not depend on $\sigma^2$:

- $(2\pi)^{-n/2}$;
- $|\mathbf R|^{-1/2}$, conditional on $\phi$; and
- $b_\sigma^{a_\sigma}/\Gamma(a_\sigma)$.

They can be absorbed into the proportionality constant. Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf W,\phi)
&\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}\\
&\quad\times
(\sigma^2)^{-a_\sigma-1}
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\sigma}{\sigma^2}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

- Combine the powers of $\sigma^2$

$$
(\sigma^2)^{-n/2}(\sigma^2)^{-a_\sigma-1}
=
(\sigma^2)^{-(a_\sigma+n/2)-1}.
$$

- Combine the exponential terms

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\sigma}{\sigma^2}\right)\\
&\qquad=
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}
\left(b_\sigma+
\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W
\right)\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

- Final unnormalised posterior

Therefore,

$$
\pi(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf W,\phi)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-(a_\sigma+n/2)-1}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}
\left(b_\sigma+
\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W
\right)\right\}.
$$

## 11.6 Recognise the Inverse-Gamma distribution

The kernel of an Inverse-Gamma distribution is

$$
x^{-\alpha-1}\exp\left(-\frac{\beta}{x}\right).
$$

Comparing this with the posterior kernel gives

$$
x=\sigma^2,
$$

$$
\alpha=a_\sigma+\frac n2,
$$

and

$$
\beta=b_\sigma+
\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W.
$$

## 11.7 Final result

The full conditional distribution for $\sigma^2$ is

$$
\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid\mathbf W,\phi
\sim
\operatorname{IG}\left(
a_\sigma+\frac n2,
b_\sigma+
\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W
\right)
}.
$$

The updated shape parameter is

$$
a^*=a_\sigma+\frac n2,
$$

and the updated scale parameter is

$$
b^*=b_\sigma+
\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W.
$$

## 11.8 Connection to the R code

- Code implementation

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Compute R^{-1} using Cholesky decomposition
R_current <- make_correlation(phi_current)
R_inverse <- chol2inv(chol(R_current))

# Calculate the quadratic form
Wt_Rinv_W <- drop(
  crossprod(W_current, R_inverse %*% W_current)
)

# Updated shape parameter
sigma2_shape <- priors$sigma2_shape + n / 2

# Updated scale for the Inverse-Gamma distribution
# This is also the rate used for the reciprocal Gamma draw.
sigma2_scale <- priors$sigma2_scale + 0.5 * Wt_Rinv_W

# If Z ~ Gamma(shape, rate), then 1/Z ~ IG(shape, scale = rate)
sigma2_current <- 1 / rgamma(
  1,
  shape = sigma2_shape,
  rate = sigma2_scale
)
```

- Mathematical equivalence

The code calculates

$$
\mathtt{sigma2\_shape}
=a_\sigma+\frac n2,
$$

and

$$
\mathtt{sigma2\_scale}
=b_\sigma+
\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W.
$$

It then generates

$$
\mathtt{sigma2\_current}
\sim
\operatorname{IG}(mathtt{sigma2\_shape},mathtt{sigma2\_scale}).
$$

## 11.9 Why we use the Inverse-Gamma distribution

- Conjugacy

The Inverse-Gamma prior is conjugate for $\sigma^2$ because:

1. the conditional model for $\mathbf W$ is Normal with covariance $\sigma^2\mathbf R$;
2. the prior for $\sigma^2$ is Inverse-Gamma; and
3. the resulting full conditional distribution is also Inverse-Gamma.

This is analogous to using:

- a Normal prior for $\boldsymbol\beta$ with a Normal likelihood, producing a Normal full conditional; and
- an Inverse-Gamma prior for $\tau^2$ in a Normal error model, producing an Inverse-Gamma full conditional.

- Properties of the Inverse-Gamma distribution

For $X\sim\operatorname{IG}(\alpha,\beta)$ under the shape--scale parameterisation used here:

| Property | Value |
|:---|:---|
| Support | $x>0$ |
| Mean | $\displaystyle \frac{\beta}{\alpha-1}$, for $\alpha>1$ |
| Mode | $\displaystyle \frac{\beta}{\alpha+1}$ |
| Variance | $\displaystyle \frac{\beta^2}{(\alpha-1)^2(\alpha-2)}$, for $\alpha>2$ |

## 11.10 Intuitive interpretation

- Shape parameter

$$
a^*=a_\sigma+\frac n2.
$$

- $a_\sigma$ represents prior information.
- $n/2$ is the contribution from the $n$-dimensional spatial random-effects vector.

- Scale parameter

$$
b^*=b_\sigma+
\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W.
$$

- $b_\sigma$ is the prior scale parameter.
- $\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W$ is the contribution from the spatial random effects.

- Interpretation of the quadratic form

The term

$$
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W
$$

is a squared Mahalanobis distance:

1. $\mathbf R^{-1}$ accounts for the correlation among the spatial random effects.
2. The quadratic form measures how large $\mathbf W$ is relative to the variation implied by $\mathbf R$.
3. A larger quadratic form leads to a larger posterior value of $b^*$ and generally supports greater spatial variance.

## 11.11 Full derivation chain

- Step 1: Model assumption

$$
\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi
\sim N_n(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2\mathbf R).
$$

- Step 2: Density of $\mathbf W$

$$
f(\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi)
=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}(\sigma^2)^{n/2}|\mathbf R|^{1/2}}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}.
$$
- Step 3: Prior for $\sigma^2$

$$
\pi(\sigma^2)
=
\frac{b_\sigma^{a_\sigma}}{\Gamma(a_\sigma)}
(\sigma^2)^{-a_\sigma-1}
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\sigma}{\sigma^2}\right).
$$

- Step 4: Apply Bayes' theorem

$$
\pi(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf W,\phi)
\propto
f(\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi)\pi(\sigma^2).
$$

- Step 5: Simplify

$$
\pi(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf W,\phi)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-(a_\sigma+n/2)-1}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}
\left(b_\sigma+
\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W
\right)\right\}.
$$

- Step 6: Recognise the Inverse-Gamma distribution

$$
\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid\mathbf W,\phi
\sim
\operatorname{IG}\left(
a_\sigma+\frac n2,
b_\sigma+
\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W
\right)
}.
$$

# 12. Mathematics of How $\tau^2$ Was Updated

## 12.1 The model and assumptions

- Data model (likelihood)

$$
\mathbf Y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W,\tau^2
\sim
N_n\left(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\mathbf W,
\tau^2\mathbf I_n\right).
$$

- Prior for $\tau^2$

Assume

$$
\tau^2\sim\operatorname{IG}(a_\tau,b_\tau),
$$

using the shape--scale form of the Inverse-Gamma distribution. Its density is

$$
\pi(\tau^2)
=
\frac{b_\tau^{a_\tau}}{\Gamma(a_\tau)}
(\tau^2)^{-a_\tau-1}
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\tau}{\tau^2}\right),
\qquad \tau^2>0,
$$

where:

- $a_\tau$ is the shape parameter; and
- $b_\tau$ is the scale parameter in this Inverse-Gamma parameterisation.

> **Parameterisation note:** In this density, $b_\tau$ is conventionally called the Inverse-Gamma scale parameter. When $\tau^2$ is generated as the reciprocal of a Gamma random variable, the same value is used as the Gamma rate.

## 12.2 The likelihood function

- Write the likelihood

From the data model, the likelihood as a function of $\tau^2$ is

$$
L(\tau^2)
=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}|\tau^2\mathbf I_n|^{1/2}}
\exp\left\{
-\frac12
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)^\mathsf T
(\tau^2\mathbf I_n)^{-1}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)
\right\}.
$$

- Simplify the determinant

Because $\mathbf I_n$ is an $n\times n$ identity matrix,

$$
|\tau^2\mathbf I_n|^{1/2}
=\left\{(\tau^2)^n\right\}^{1/2}
=(\tau^2)^{n/2}
=\tau^n.
$$

- Simplify the inverse

$$
(\tau^2\mathbf I_n)^{-1}
=\frac{1}{\tau^2}\mathbf I_n.
$$

- Simplify the quadratic form

Define the residual vector

$$
\mathbf r
=\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W.
$$

Then

$$
\mathbf r^\mathsf T
(\tau^2\mathbf I_n)^{-1}\mathbf r
=\frac{1}{\tau^2}\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r.
$$

- Final likelihood

Therefore,

$$
L(\tau^2)
=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}(\tau^2)^{n/2}}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)^\mathsf T
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)
\right\}.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
L(\tau^2)
=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}(\tau^2)^{n/2}}
\exp\left(-\frac{\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r}{2\tau^2}\right).
$$

## 12.3 The prior for $\tau^2$

The Inverse-Gamma prior is

$$
\pi(\tau^2)
=
\frac{b_\tau^{a_\tau}}{\Gamma(a_\tau)}
(\tau^2)^{-a_\tau-1}
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\tau}{\tau^2}\right).
$$

## 12.4 Combine the likelihood and prior

By Bayes' theorem,

$$
\pi(\tau^2\mid\mathbf Y,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W)
\propto
L(\tau^2)\pi(\tau^2).
$$

- Write the unnormalised posterior

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi(\tau^2\mid\mathbf Y,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W)
&\propto
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}(\tau^2)^{n/2}}
\exp\left(-\frac{\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r}{2\tau^2}\right)\\
&\quad\times
\frac{b_\tau^{a_\tau}}{\Gamma(a_\tau)}
(\tau^2)^{-a_\tau-1}
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\tau}{\tau^2}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

- Drop constants not involving $\tau^2$

The terms $(2\pi)^{-n/2}$ and $b_\tau^{a_\tau}/\Gamma(a_\tau)$ do not depend on $\tau^2$. They can be absorbed into the proportionality constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi(\tau^2\mid\mathbf Y,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W)
&\propto
(\tau^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left(-\frac{\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r}{2\tau^2}\right)\\
&\quad\times
(\tau^2)^{-a_\tau-1}
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\tau}{\tau^2}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

- Combine the powers of $\tau^2$

$$
(\tau^2)^{-n/2}(\tau^2)^{-a_\tau-1}
=
(\tau^2)^{-(a_\tau+n/2)-1}.
$$

- Combine the exponential terms

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\exp\left(-\frac{\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r}{2\tau^2}\right)
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\tau}{\tau^2}\right)\\
&\qquad=
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{\tau^2}
\left(b_\tau+\frac12\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r\right)
\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

- Final unnormalised posterior

Thus,

$$
\pi(\tau^2\mid\mathbf Y,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W)
\propto
(\tau^2)^{-(a_\tau+n/2)-1}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{\tau^2}
\left(b_\tau+\frac12\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r\right)
\right\}.
$$

Substituting $\mathbf r=\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi(\tau^2\mid\mathbf Y,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W)
&\propto
(\tau^2)^{-(a_\tau+n/2)-1}\\
&\quad\times
\exp\left[
-\frac{1}{\tau^2}
\left\{
b_\tau+
\frac12
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)^\mathsf T
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)
\right\}
\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

## 12.5 Recognise the Inverse-Gamma distribution

For

$$
X\sim\operatorname{IG}(\alpha,\beta),
$$

the density kernel is

$$
x^{-\alpha-1}\exp\left(-\frac{\beta}{x}\right).
$$

Matching this kernel with the posterior gives

$$
x=\tau^2,
$$

$$
\alpha=a_\tau+\frac n2,
$$

and

$$
\beta=b_\tau+\frac12\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r.
$$

## 12.5 Final result

The full conditional distribution for $\tau^2$ is

$$
\boxed{
\tau^2\mid\mathbf Y,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W
\sim
\operatorname{IG}\left[
a_\tau+\frac n2,
b_\tau+
\frac12
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)^\mathsf T
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)
\right]
}.
$$

The updated shape parameter is

$$
a^*=a_\tau+\frac n2,
$$

and the updated scale parameter is

$$
b^*=b_\tau+\frac12\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r,
$$

where

$$
\mathbf r=\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W.
$$

## 12.6 Comparison with $\sigma^2$

- Similarities

Both $\sigma^2$ and $\tau^2$ have Inverse-Gamma full conditional distributions.

| Parameter | Updated shape | Updated scale |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| $\sigma^2$ | $a_\sigma+n/2$ | $b_\sigma+\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W$ |
| $\tau^2$ | $a_\tau+n/2$ | $b_\tau+\frac12(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)^\mathsf T(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W)$ |

- Differences

| Aspect | $\sigma^2$ | $\tau^2$ |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Source | Spatial process | Independent error |
| Quadratic form | $\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf W$ | $\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r$ |
| Correlation | Includes spatial correlation through $\mathbf R$ | Assumes independent errors through $\mathbf I_n$ |
| Interpretation | Spatial variance | Nugget variance |

## 12.7 Connection to the R code

- Code implementation

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Compute residuals
residual <- as.numeric(
  Y - X %*% beta_current - W_current
)

# Updated shape parameter
tau2_shape <- priors$tau2_shape + n / 2

# Updated Inverse-Gamma scale
# This is also the rate for the reciprocal Gamma draw.
tau2_scale <- priors$tau2_scale +
  0.5 * sum(residual^2)

# Sample from the Inverse-Gamma distribution
tau2_current <- 1 / rgamma(
  1,
  shape = tau2_shape,
  rate = tau2_scale
)
```

- Mathematical equivalence

The code calculates

$$
\mathtt{tau2\_shape}
=a_\tau+\frac n2,
$$

and

$$
\mathtt{tau2\_scale}
=b_\tau+\frac12\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r.
$$

It then generates

$$
\mathtt{tau2\_current}
\sim
\operatorname{IG}(mathtt{tau2\_shape},mathtt{tau2\_scale}).
$$

## 12.8 Step-by-step explanation of the code

- Line 1: Compute the residuals

```{r, eval=FALSE}
residual <- as.numeric(
  Y - X %*% beta_current - W_current
)
```

Mathematically,

$$
\mathbf r=\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf W.
$$

This calculation:

- removes the mean trend $\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$;
- removes the spatial random effects $\mathbf W$; and
- leaves the independent errors $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$.

- Line 2: Update the shape parameter

```{r, eval=FALSE}
tau2_shape <- priors$tau2_shape + n / 2
```

Mathematically,

$$
a^*=a_\tau+\frac n2.
$$

The $n/2$ term arises from the factor $(\tau^2)^{-n/2}$ in the Normal likelihood.

- Line 3: Update the scale parameter

```{r, eval=FALSE}
tau2_scale <- priors$tau2_scale +
  0.5 * sum(residual^2)
```

Mathematically,

$$
b^*=b_\tau+\frac12\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r.
$$

Here:

- `sum(residual^2)` equals $\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r$;
- the sum of squared residuals is multiplied by $1/2$; and
- the result is added to the prior scale parameter.
- Line 4: Sample $\tau^2$

```{r, eval=FALSE}
tau2_current <- 1 / rgamma(
  1,
  shape = tau2_shape,
  rate = tau2_scale
)
```

If

$$
Z\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a^*,\text{rate}=b^*),
$$

then

$$
\frac{1}{Z}\sim\operatorname{IG}(a^*,\text{scale}=b^*).
$$

Therefore, `1 / rgamma()` generates the required Inverse-Gamma draw for $\tau^2$.

## 12.9 Full derivation chain

- Step 1: Model assumption

$$
\mathbf Y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W,\tau^2
\sim
N_n(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\mathbf W,\tau^2\mathbf I_n).
$$

- Step 2: Likelihood for $\tau^2$

$$
L(\tau^2)
\propto
(\tau^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left(-\frac{\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r}{2\tau^2}\right).
$$

- Step 3: Prior for $\tau^2$

$$
\pi(\tau^2)
\propto
(\tau^2)^{-a_\tau-1}
\exp\left(-\frac{b_\tau}{\tau^2}\right).
$$

- Step 4: Apply Bayes' theorem

$$
\pi(\tau^2\mid\mathbf Y,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W)
\propto
L(\tau^2)\pi(\tau^2).
$$

- Step 5: Simplify

$$
\pi(\tau^2\mid\mathbf Y,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W)
\propto
(\tau^2)^{-(a_\tau+n/2)-1}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{\tau^2}
\left(b_\tau+\frac12\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r\right)
\right\}.
$$
- Step 6: Recognise the Inverse-Gamma distribution

$$
\boxed{
\tau^2\mid\mathbf Y,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf W
\sim
\operatorname{IG}\left(
a_\tau+\frac n2,
b_\tau+\frac12\mathbf r^\mathsf T\mathbf r
\right)
}.
$$
#  13 Mathematics as How $\phi$ was updated

## 13.1 The model and assumptions

### 13.1.1 Process model: prior for $\mathbf W$

$$
\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi
\sim
N_n\left\{\mathbf 0,\sigma^2\mathbf R(\phi)\right\}.
$$

### 13.1.2 Prior for $\phi$

Assume

$$
\phi\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_\phi,b_\phi),
$$

where $a_\phi$ is the shape and $b_\phi$ is the rate. The prior density is

$$
\pi(\phi)
=\frac{b_\phi^{a_\phi}}{\Gamma(a_\phi)}
\phi^{a_\phi-1}\exp(-b_\phi\phi),
\qquad \phi>0.
$$

### 13.1.3 The prior density for $\mathbf W$

From the process model,

$$
f(\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi)
=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}|\sigma^2\mathbf R(\phi)|^{1/2}}
\exp\left\{-\frac12\mathbf W^\mathsf T
[\sigma^2\mathbf R(\phi)]^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}.
$$

- Simplify the determinant

$$
|\sigma^2\mathbf R(\phi)|^{1/2}
=\left\{(\sigma^2)^n|\mathbf R(\phi)|\right\}^{1/2}
=(\sigma^2)^{n/2}|\mathbf R(\phi)|^{1/2}.
$$

- Simplify the inverse

$$
[\sigma^2\mathbf R(\phi)]^{-1}
=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}.
$$

- Substitute

Therefore,

$$
f(\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi)
=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}(\sigma^2)^{n/2}|\mathbf R(\phi)|^{1/2}}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}.
$$

### 13.1.4 The prior for $\phi$

The Gamma prior is

$$
\pi(\phi)
=\frac{b_\phi^{a_\phi}}{\Gamma(a_\phi)}
\phi^{a_\phi-1}\exp(-b_\phi\phi).
$$

### 13.1.5 Apply Bayes' theorem

By Bayes' theorem,

$$
\pi(\phi\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)
\propto
f(\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi)\pi(\phi).
$$

- Write the unnormalised posterior

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi(\phi\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)
&\propto
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}(\sigma^2)^{n/2}|\mathbf R(\phi)|^{1/2}}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}\\
&\quad\times
\frac{b_\phi^{a_\phi}}{\Gamma(a_\phi)}
\phi^{a_\phi-1}\exp(-b_\phi\phi).
\end{aligned}
$$

- Drop constants not involving $\phi$

Conditional on $\mathbf W$ and $\sigma^2$, the following terms do not depend on $\phi$:

- $(2\pi)^{-n/2}$;
- $(\sigma^2)^{-n/2}$; and
- $b_\phi^{a_\phi}/\Gamma(a_\phi)$.

After dropping them,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi(\phi\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)
&\propto
|\mathbf R(\phi)|^{-1/2}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}\\
&\quad\times
\phi^{a_\phi-1}\exp(-b_\phi\phi).
\end{aligned}
$$

- Combine the exponential terms

$$
\pi(\phi\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)
\propto
|\mathbf R(\phi)|^{-1/2}
\phi^{a_\phi-1}
\exp\left\{-b_\phi\phi
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}\mathbf W
\right\}.
$$

- Final unnormalised posterior

The full conditional kernel is

$$
\boxed{
\pi(\phi\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)
\propto
|\mathbf R(\phi)|^{-1/2}
\phi^{a_\phi-1}
\exp\left\{-b_\phi\phi
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}\mathbf W
\right\}
}.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\pi(\phi\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)
\propto
|\sigma^2\mathbf R(\phi)|^{-1/2}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}
\pi(\phi).
$$

### 13.1.6 Why this has no standard closed form

$\phi$ appears nonlinearly in several parts of the conditional density.

| Term | How $\phi$ appears | Why it is problematic |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $|\mathbf R(\phi)|^{-1/2}$ | Inside the determinant of a correlation matrix | The determinant is a nonlinear function of $\phi$ |
| $\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}$ | Inside a matrix inverse | Every element of the inverse generally changes with $\phi$ |
| $\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}\mathbf W$ | Inside a quadratic form | It is a nonlinear function of $\phi$ |

### 13.1.7 Determinant term

If $\lambda_i(\phi)$ is the $i$th eigenvalue of $\mathbf R(\phi)$, then

$$
|\mathbf R(\phi)|
=\prod_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(\phi).
$$

Every eigenvalue can depend on $\phi$ in a complicated way.

### 13.1.8 Inverse term

Using an eigendecomposition,

$$
\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}
=\mathbf U(\phi)\boldsymbol\Lambda(\phi)^{-1}
\mathbf U(\phi)^\mathsf T,
$$

where both the eigenvectors and eigenvalues can depend on $\phi$.

### 13.1.9 Quadratic form

The quadratic form can be written as

$$
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}\mathbf W
=\sum_{i=1}^n
\frac{[\mathbf u_i(\phi)^\mathsf T\mathbf W]^2}
{\lambda_i(\phi)}.
$$

Thus, it is a sum of terms whose numerators and denominators may both depend on $\phi$.

## 13.2 Comparison with the other parameters

| Parameter | Full conditional | Sampling method | Reason |
|:---:|:---|:---|:---|
| $\boldsymbol\beta$ | Multivariate Normal | Gibbs | Normal conjugacy |
| $\mathbf W$ | Multivariate Normal | Gibbs | Normal conjugacy |
| $\sigma^2$ | Inverse-Gamma | Gibbs | Inverse-Gamma conjugacy |
| $\tau^2$ | Inverse-Gamma | Gibbs | Inverse-Gamma conjugacy |
| $\phi$ | Nonstandard | Metropolis--Hastings | No standard conjugate form |

For $\phi$,

$$
f(\mathbf W\mid\sigma^2,\phi)
\propto
|\mathbf R(\phi)|^{-1/2}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}.
$$

Multiplying this expression by a Gamma prior does not produce a standard named distribution.

## 13.3 The Metropolis--Hastings solution

Metropolis--Hastings only requires the unnormalised target density. Define

$$
h(\phi)
=|\sigma^2\mathbf R(\phi)|^{-1/2}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}\mathbf W\right\}
\pi(\phi).
$$

Then

$$
\pi(\phi\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)\propto h(\phi).
$$

- Metropolis--Hastings algorithm

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Step 1: Transform to the unconstrained log scale
eta_current <- log(phi_current)

# Step 2: Propose a new value
eta_proposed <- rnorm(
  1,
  mean = eta_current,
  sd = phi_proposal_sd
)

# Step 3: Transform back
phi_proposed <- exp(eta_proposed)

# Step 4: Compute log target densities on the eta scale
log_target_current <-
  log_conditional(W, sigma2, phi_current) + eta_current

log_target_proposed <-
  log_conditional(W, sigma2, phi_proposed) + eta_proposed

# Step 5: Compute the log acceptance ratio
log_acceptance_ratio <-
  log_target_proposed - log_target_current

# Step 6: Accept or reject
if (log(runif(1)) < log_acceptance_ratio) {
  phi_current <- phi_proposed
}
```

- R code implementment

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Random-walk MH on eta = log(phi)
eta_current <- log(phi_current)
eta_proposed <- rnorm(
  1,
  mean = eta_current,
  sd = phi_proposal_sd
)

phi_proposed <- exp(eta_proposed)
R_proposed <- make_correlation(phi_proposed)

# Log target for the current value
log_target_current <- dmvnorm(
  W_current,
  mean = rep(0, n),
  sigma = sigma2_current * R_current,
  log = TRUE
) + dgamma(
  phi_current,
  shape = priors$phi_shape,
  rate = priors$phi_rate,
  log = TRUE
) + eta_current

# Log target for the proposed value
log_target_proposed <- dmvnorm(
  W_current,
  mean = rep(0, n),
  sigma = sigma2_current * R_proposed,
  log = TRUE
) + dgamma(
  phi_proposed,
  shape = priors$phi_shape,
  rate = priors$phi_rate,
  log = TRUE
) + eta_proposed

# Accept or reject
log_acceptance_ratio <-
  log_target_proposed - log_target_current

if (
  is.finite(log_acceptance_ratio) &&
  log(runif(1)) < log_acceptance_ratio
) {
  phi_current <- phi_proposed
  R_current <- R_proposed
  phi_accepted[i] <- TRUE
}
```

## 13.4 Mathematical equivalence

The multivariate Normal log density contributes

$$
-\frac12\log|\sigma^2\mathbf R(\phi)|
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\mathbf W^\mathsf T\mathbf R(\phi)^{-1}\mathbf W
+\text{constant}.
$$

The Gamma log prior contributes

$$
(a_\phi-1)\log\phi-b_\phi\phi+\text{constant}.
$$

The term $\eta=\log\phi$ is the log-Jacobian adjustment for transforming the target density from $\phi$ to $\eta$.

## 13.5 A complete example

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Setup
set.seed(123)
n <- 20
coords <- matrix(runif(2 * n), ncol = 2)
dist_mat <- as.matrix(dist(coords))

# True parameters
sigma2_true <- 0.8
phi_true <- 1.5

# Generate W
R <- exp(-dist_mat / phi_true)
L <- chol(sigma2_true * R)
W <- as.numeric(t(L) %*% rnorm(n))

# Prior parameters
priors <- list(phi_shape = 2, phi_rate = 1)

# Compute the unnormalised log conditional density
log_conditional <- function(phi) {
  R <- exp(-dist_mat / phi)
  R_inv <- chol2inv(chol(R))

  log_det <- -0.5 * as.numeric(
    determinant(R, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus
  )

  quad_form <- -0.5 * drop(
    crossprod(W, R_inv %*% W)
  ) / sigma2_true

  log_prior <- dgamma(
    phi,
    shape = priors$phi_shape,
    rate = priors$phi_rate,
    log = TRUE
  )

  log_det + quad_form + log_prior
}

# Evaluate the density on a grid
phi_grid <- seq(0.1, 5, length.out = 100)
log_density <- sapply(phi_grid, log_conditional)
density <- exp(log_density - max(log_density))

# Plot
plot(
  phi_grid,
  density,
  type = "l",
  lwd = 2,
  main = expression("Unnormalised posterior of " * phi),
  xlab = expression(phi),
  ylab = "Relative density"
)

abline(v = phi_true, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = expression("True " * phi),
  col = "red",
  lty = 2,
  lwd = 2
)
```

## 13.5 Why transform to the log scale?

- Problem with sampling $\phi$ directly

- $\phi$ must be positive: $\phi>0$.
- A Normal random-walk proposal on the original scale can generate negative values.
- Negative proposed values are outside the support of $\phi$.

- Log transformation

Define

$$
\eta=\log\phi.
$$

Then:

- $\eta$ is unconstrained, with $\eta\in(-\infty,\infty)$;
- a Normal proposal for $\eta$ always produces a positive $\phi^*=\exp(\eta^*)$; and
- the transformed target includes a Jacobian adjustment.

## 13.6 Jacobian adjustment

Since

$$
\phi=e^\eta,
\qquad
\frac{d\phi}{d\eta}=e^\eta,
$$

the transformed density is

$$
\pi_\eta(\eta\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)
=\pi_\phi(e^\eta\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)e^\eta.
$$

On the log scale,

$$
\log\pi_\eta(\eta\mid\cdot)
=\log\pi_\phi(e^\eta\mid\cdot)+\eta.
$$

Therefore, the code includes `+ eta_current` and `+ eta_proposed`.

## 13.7 The acceptance ratio

The Metropolis--Hastings acceptance probability on the transformed scale is

$$
\alpha
=\min\left\{
1,
\frac{\pi_\eta(\eta^*\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)
q(\eta\mid\eta^*)}
{\pi_\eta(\eta\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)
q(\eta^*\mid\eta)}
\right\}.
$$

The Normal random-walk proposal is symmetric:

$$
q(\eta^*\mid\eta)=q(\eta\mid\eta^*).
$$

Consequently,

$$
\alpha
=\min\left\{
1,
\frac{\pi_\phi(\phi^*\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)\phi^*}
{\pi_\phi(\phi\mid\mathbf W,\sigma^2)\phi}
\right\}.
$$

Equivalently, the log acceptance ratio is

$$
\log A
=\log\pi_\phi(\phi^*\mid\cdot)
-\log\pi_\phi(\phi\mid\cdot)
+\eta^*-\eta.
$$

The proposed value is accepted when

$$
\log U<\log A,
\qquad U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).
$$

## 13.8 Summary

| Aspect | $\boldsymbol\beta$, $\mathbf W$, $\sigma^2$, $\tau^2$ | $\phi$ |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Full conditional | Standard closed form | Nonstandard form |
| Distribution | Normal or Inverse-Gamma | No standard named distribution |
| Sampling | Gibbs sampling | Metropolis--Hastings |
| Reason | Conjugacy | No standard conjugate prior |
| Acceptance | Direct draw | Proposed draw may be rejected |
| Tuning | None for direct Gibbs draw | Proposal standard deviation required |



# 14 Fit the spatial models using above R code

## 14.1 Fit exponential spatial model
```{r, message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}

# FIT EXPONENTIAL SPATIAL MODEL 

set.seed(54321)


priors_default <- list(
  beta_mean = 0,
  beta_var = 1000,
  sigma2_shape = 2,
  sigma2_rate = 1,
  tau2_shape = 2,
  tau2_rate = 1,
  phi_shape = 2,
  phi_rate = 1
)

mcmc_exp <- run_spatial_mcmc(
  data = litho2,
  response = "log_Thickness",
  covariates = c(
    "Surf_Elevation_scaled",
    "AB_Elevation_scaled"
  ),
  coords = litho2[, c("Easting", "Northing")],
  n_iter = 10000,
  burnin = 5000,
  thin = 5,
  cov_family = "exponential",
  priors = priors_default,
  initial_values = list(
    beta = NULL,
    W = NULL,
    sigma2 = 0.5,
    tau2 = 0.2,
    phi = 1
  ),
  phi_proposal_sd = 0.15,
  progress_every = 1000
)
```

## 14.3  Function for posterior summary and diagnosie

```{r, message=FALSE, warnging=FALSE}

# POSTERIOR SUMMARY AND DIAGNOSTICS 

summarise_mcmc_model <- function(fit, model_name) {
  posterior_matrix <- as.matrix(fit$samples)

  posterior_summary <- t(apply(
    posterior_matrix,
    2,
    function(x) {
      c(
        Mean = mean(x),
        SD = sd(x),
        Median = median(x),
        `2.5%` = unname(quantile(x, 0.025)),
        `97.5%` = unname(quantile(x, 0.975))
      )
    }
  ))

  cat("\n===", toupper(model_name), "POSTERIOR SUMMARY ===\n")
  print(round(posterior_summary, 4))

  cat(
    "\n", model_name, "phi acceptance rate:",
    round(fit$acceptance_rate, 3), "\n"
  )

  if (fit$acceptance_rate < 0.20) {
    cat("Acceptance is low: consider reducing phi_proposal_sd.\n")
  } else if (fit$acceptance_rate > 0.50) {
    cat("Acceptance is high: consider increasing phi_proposal_sd.\n")
  } else {
    cat("The phi acceptance rate is in a reasonable range.\n")
  }

  # These diagnostics are protected so that a degenerate chain cannot
  # destroy the fitted model object.
  effective_sample_sizes <- tryCatch(
    coda::effectiveSize(fit$samples),
    error = function(e) {
      warning(model_name, " effectiveSize failed: ", conditionMessage(e))
      setNames(rep(NA_real_, ncol(posterior_matrix)), colnames(posterior_matrix))
    }
  )

  cat("\n===", toupper(model_name), "EFFECTIVE SAMPLE SIZES ===\n")
  print(effective_sample_sizes)

  autocorrelation <- tryCatch(
    coda::autocorr.diag(fit$samples, lags = c(1, 5, 10, 20)),
    error = function(e) {
      warning(model_name, " autocorr.diag failed: ", conditionMessage(e))
      NULL
    }
  )

  if (!is.null(autocorrelation)) {
    cat("\n===", toupper(model_name), "AUTOCORRELATIONS ===\n")
    print(round(autocorrelation, 3))
  }

  list(
    posterior_matrix = posterior_matrix,
    posterior_summary = posterior_summary,
    effective_sample_sizes = effective_sample_sizes,
    autocorrelation = autocorrelation
  )
}

```

## 14.4 Results for exponential spatial model

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

options(scipen = 999)
diagnostics_exp <- summarise_mcmc_model(mcmc_exp, "Exponential")
diagnostics_exp
plot( mcmc_exp$samples[, c( "beta_0", "beta_1", "beta_2" )])
plot( mcmc_exp$samples[, c(  "sigma2", "tau2", "phi")])


```

## 14.5 Results for Matern spatial model

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

diagnostics_matern
plot( mcmc_matern$samples[, c( "beta_0", "beta_1", "beta_2" )])
```
