# 15 Use R package spBayes to fit the Bayesian spatial regression model

In fact, we do not need to write our own R function to conduct the Bayesian spatial regression models. Below we use spBayes::spLM() to run the analysis.


## 15.1 Prepare coordinates

The coordinates should be rescaled because large coordinate values can make the spatial decay parameter difficult to estimate.


```{r, message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}

# PREPARE COORDINATES ----------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(spBayes)
library(coda)
# Convert coordinates to kilometres if the original units are metres
coords <- as.matrix(
  litho2[, c("Easting", "Northing")]
) / 1000

colnames(coords) <- c("Easting_km", "Northing_km")

# Maximum pairwise distance
max_distance <- max(spBayes::iDist(coords))

max_distance

```

In **spBayes**, the exponential correlation function is parameterised as

$$R_{ij} = \exp(-\phi d_{ij}).$$

Therefore, $\phi$ is a spatial decay parameter. This differs from your custom function, which used

$$R_{ij} = \exp\left(-\frac{\phi}{\text{range}} d_{ij}\right).$$

The two parameters are related by

$$\phi_{\text{spBayes}} = \frac{1}{\phi_{\text{range}}}.$$

For the exponential covariance, the practical spatial range—where correlation is approximately 0.05—is

$$d_{0.05} \approx \frac{3}{\phi}.$$

## 15.2 Priors and starting values

`spLM()` uses:

- $\sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(a_\sigma, b_\sigma)$
- $\tau^2 \sim \text{IG}(a_\tau, b_\tau)$

and a **Uniform** prior for $\phi$.


```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# PRIOR AND MCMC SETTINGS ------------------------------------------

response_variance <- var(litho2$log_Thickness)

# Phi bounds based on the maximum distance
phi_lower <- 3 / max_distance
phi_upper <- 300 / max_distance

# Starting value corresponding to an effective range
# of approximately half the maximum distance
phi_start <- 3 / (0.5 * max_distance)

starting_common <- list(
  sigma.sq = 0.7 * response_variance,
  tau.sq = 0.3 * response_variance,
  phi = phi_start
)

tuning_common <- list(
  sigma.sq = 0.05,
  tau.sq = 0.05,
  phi = 0.05
)

priors_common <- list(
  sigma.sq.ig = c(0.1, 0.1),
  tau.sq.ig = c(0.1, 0.1),
  phi.unif = c(phi_lower, phi_upper)
)

starting_common
priors_common


```

Unlike THE custom model, spLM() does not provide a Gamma prior for $\phi$; it uses a Uniform prior for the spatial decay parameter. The inverse-Gamma priors for the two variance components remain the same.


## 15.3 Exponential covariance model

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# FIT EXPONENTIAL COVARIANCE MODEL ---------------------------------

set.seed(2026)

fit_exponential <- spLM(
  log_Thickness ~
    Surf_Elevation_scaled +
    AB_Elevation_scaled,

  data = litho2,
  coords = coords,

  starting = starting_common,
  tuning = tuning_common,
  priors = priors_common,

  cov.model = "exponential",

  n.samples = 30000,
  verbose = TRUE,
  n.report = 1000
)
```

The fitted object initially contains samples for the covariance parameters:

```{r}
names(fit_exponential)
summary(fit_exponential$p.theta.samples)

```

Recover the regression coefficients and spatial random effects after discarding the first 10,000 iterations and retaining every tenth sample:

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
fit_exponential <- spRecover(
  fit_exponential,
  start = 10001,
  end = 30000,
  thin = 10,
  get.beta = TRUE,
  get.w = TRUE,
  verbose = TRUE,
  n.report = 500
)

```

## 15.4 Matérn covariance model

For the Matérn model, fix the smoothness parameter at

$$\nu=1.5$$.

Setting its tuning variance to zero tells spLM() not to update it.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# 6. FIT MATERN COVARIANCE MODEL --------------------------------------

starting_matern <- c(
  starting_common,
  list(nu = 1.5)
)

tuning_matern <- c(
  tuning_common,
  list(nu = 0)
)

priors_matern <- c(
  priors_common,
  list(nu.unif = c(0.5, 2.5))
)

set.seed(2026)

fit_matern <- spLM(
  log_Thickness ~
    Surf_Elevation_scaled +
    AB_Elevation_scaled,

  data = litho2,
  coords = coords,

  starting = starting_matern,
  tuning = tuning_matern,
  priors = priors_matern,

  cov.model = "matern",

  n.samples = 30000,
  verbose = TRUE,
  n.report = 1000
)

fit_matern <- spRecover(
  fit_matern,
  start = 10001,
  end = 30000,
  thin = 10,
  get.beta = TRUE,
  get.w = TRUE,
  verbose = TRUE,
  n.report = 500
)
```

## 15.5 Posterior summaries

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# 7. POSTERIOR SUMMARIES ----------------------------------------------

cat("\nExponential covariance parameters\n")

summary(
  window(
    fit_exponential$p.theta.samples,
    start = 10001,
    thin = 10
  )
)

cat("\nExponential regression coefficients\n")

summary(
  fit_exponential$p.beta.recover.samples
)


cat("\nMatérn covariance parameters\n")

summary(
  window(
    fit_matern$p.theta.samples,
    start = 10001,
    thin = 10
  )
)

cat("\nMatérn regression coefficients\n")

summary(
  fit_matern$p.beta.recover.samples
)
```

# 15.6 Create a concise posterior summary table:

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
posterior_summary <- function(samples, model_name) {

  samples <- as.matrix(samples)

  tibble(
    Model = model_name,
    Parameter = colnames(samples),
    Mean = apply(samples, 2, mean),
    SD = apply(samples, 2, sd),
    Median = apply(samples, 2, median),
    Lower_95 = apply(
      samples,
      2,
      quantile,
      probs = 0.025
    ),
    Upper_95 = apply(
      samples,
      2,
      quantile,
      probs = 0.975
    )
  )
}

beta_summary <- bind_rows(
  posterior_summary(
    fit_exponential$p.beta.recover.samples,
    "Exponential"
  ),
  posterior_summary(
    fit_matern$p.beta.recover.samples,
    "Matern"
  )
)

beta_summary
```

```

```

## 15.7 MCMC diagnostic plots

Each parameter will have its own trace plot and posterior density plot. The model name should be used as the overall title, not as the name of every parameter.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# 8. MCMC DIAGNOSTICS -------------------------------------------------

theta_exp <- window(
  fit_exponential$p.theta.samples,
  start = 10001,
  thin = 10
)

theta_mat <- window(
  fit_matern$p.theta.samples,
  start = 10001,
  thin = 10
)

# Exponential covariance parameters
plot(
  theta_exp
  )

# Exponential regression coefficients
plot(
  fit_exponential$p.beta.recover.samples
)

# Matérn covariance parameters
par(mar = c(2, 2, 2, 2))
plot(
  theta_mat
  )


# Matérn regression coefficients
plot(
  fit_matern$p.beta.recover.samples
 )
```

## 15.8 Additional numerical diagnostics

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Effective sample sizes
effectiveSize(theta_exp)
effectiveSize(theta_mat)

effectiveSize(
  fit_exponential$p.beta.recover.samples
)

effectiveSize(
  fit_matern$p.beta.recover.samples
)

# Geweke convergence diagnostics
geweke.diag(theta_exp)
geweke.diag(theta_mat)

geweke.diag(
  fit_exponential$p.beta.recover.samples
)

geweke.diag(
  fit_matern$p.beta.recover.samples
)

```

## 15.9 Convert $\phi$ into practical spatial range
For the exponential model:
```{r, message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
phi_exp <- as.matrix(theta_exp)[, "phi"]

effective_range_exp <- 3 / phi_exp

quantile(
  effective_range_exp,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)
)
```

This is now a package-based analysis: spLM() performs the MCMC estimation, while  spRecover() generates posterior samples for $\beta$ and W(s). The current spBayes documentation confirms that spLM() supports exponential and Matérn covariance models, inverse-Gamma priors for $\sigma^2$ and $\tau^2$, a Uniform prior for phi, and a flat default prior for the regression coefficients.
